newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Kohl due in Prague to sign Czech-German accord.
newsitem.headline: Kohl due in Prague to sign Czech-German accord.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl was due in Prague on Tuesday to sign a controversial post-war accord between the Czech Republic and Germany, which both countries say is important for future European integration.
Kohl, on his first visit to an independent Czech Republic, was scheduled to sign the Czech-German declaration with Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus at 4.15 p.m. (1515 GMT).

The deal, agreed after two years of talks, is intended to help heal the wounds of World War Two and its aftermath. It also includes German support for Czech membership of the European Union and North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO).
Czech officials hope the declaration, and a speech by Kohl, will give fresh impetus to their membership hopes.

"For us it is very important because we would like to look with our German friends and colleagues towards the future and for us the main goal for the future is EU and NATO membership," said Foreign Ministry spokesman Vit Kurfurst. "Of course, there are questions connected with our past."

Germany has been the chief political sponsor of the integration with the West of post-communist East European states. The Czech Republic, along with Poland and Hungary, are the leading contenders to join both the EU and NATO.
However, Prague is the only one of Germany's neighbours not to have signed a post-war reconciliation pact with Bonn.
In the accord, Bonn expresses sorrow for the 1938-45 Nazi occupation of the Czech lands and Prague its regret for Czech brutality in the post-war expulsion of Sudeten Germans.
The declaration is highly controversial in both countries.
Czech communists and ultra-right Republicans plan demonstrations against the declaration outside the Liechtenstein Palace, where the accord is to be signed.
The communists say the deal is a sign of German domination of its neighbour. Spokeswoman Vera Zezulkova said the party had collected thousands of signatures against the accord.

"The text does not follow the interests of the Czech state and of its citizens and the results violate the sovereignty and independence of the state...The text equates Nazi crimes and the post-war consequences," she said.
The declaration has still to be ratified by both countries' parliaments.
Families and supporters of the 2.5 million expelled Germans, mostly living in Bavaria, have attacked the deal as it does not include direct compensation for confiscated property.
The two states pledge to set up a 160 million mark "Future Fund", mostly from Germany and mainly to help victims of Nazi aggression.
Kohl is scheduled to meet Czech Catholic leader Cardinal Miloslav Vlk on Wednesday and to have a private lunch with President Vaclav Havel before returning to Germany.
